outputs.L1:
Here is a polished rendition of your poem, preserving its original meaning and structure while refining the language and flow:

---

Now Spring appears, in beauty crowned,
And light and life pervade around,
Why comes not Jane? When friendship's call
Should draw her from Augusta's wall?
Where cooling zephyrs faintly sigh,
Nor spread that glow of health so nigh,
Which courses through each waking vein,
As o'er the spacious, sunlit plain
We wander forth with joyous eyes,
Beholding naught but boundless skies.

Already April's reign has fled,
Her evening splendors now are dead;
No more the violet scents the air,
No more the mists the valleys wear;
That lovely queen of smiles and tears,
Who gave thee birth, no more appears;
But blushing May, with brow serene,
And robes arrayed in livelier green,
Commands the feathered choir to sing,
Till wild, sweet notes through meadows ring.

O come! before the season's flown,
No more to greet thy twenty-one;
That age which nobler honor wears,
And fitly crowns the wreath it bears.
From languor and from cities flee,
And breathe the air of heaven with me.

---

**Key refinements made:**
- Strengthened verbs and imagery (e.g., "pervade" instead of "is," "sigh" instead of "blow") for greater lyrical elegance
- Improved grammatical consistency (e.g., "joyous eyes" instead of "joyous eye")
- Enhanced word choices for a more refined, classical tone (e.g., "splendors" for "tints," "feathered choir" for "winged choir")
- Maintained the original rhyme scheme, meter, and all factual/narrative content, including the references to Jane, Augusta, the coming of May, and the twenty-first birthday

Let me know if you'd like a version with a different tone (more modern, more formal, or more romantic) or adjustments to specific lines.

outputs.L3:
# A Letter to Jane

The garden gate stands open now, and every path I wander seems to whisper your name back to me. Spring has come into her fullness at last—the trees heavy with blossom, the fields wearing their new green like a coronation robe—and I find myself asking, again and again, why you have not come.

Jane, what keeps you bound within Augusta's walls when the whole world outside is calling? Surely you can hear it too—that persistent, tender summons that friendship sends across the miles. It asks so little: only that you answer, only that you come.

April has already slipped away from us, taking with it so much that I loved. The violets have surrendered their fragrance to memory now, and the misty vales that once wore morning veils so beautifully have dried beneath the strengthening sun. April was always a season of contradictions—smiles caught in the same breath as tears, sweetness shadowed faintly by sorrow—and now it has gone, folding all that bittersweet beauty into the past.

But May has arrived to take her place, and she comes with no melancholy in her train. Hers is a serene and confident brightness, a clarity of light that April could never quite achieve. The greenery she commands is richer, deeper, more sure of itself, and she has summoned the birds to their proper work—filling every meadow with song, until the air itself seems to hum with life and welcome.

It is into this season, Jane, that I long for you to step. Your twenty-first birthday is nearly here, and I cannot bear the thought of its passing without you beside me. Leave behind the weariness of the city—its noise, its narrow streets, its endless small demands—and come let the country air restore you. Come let us celebrate together, out where the light falls soft and unhurried, out where May is singing. The season will not wait forever. Come now, while it still remembers how to be beautiful.
outputs.L4:
**To Jane, on Her One-and-Twentieth Year**

Oh, Jane! how long shall Augusta's walls
Confine thee from the waiting world outside,
While April's frost to fainter fervor falls
And May comes forth in all her verdant pride?

I miss thee, friend—thy laughter and thy grace
Have left a silence where thy voice should be;
The very streets seem stripped of warmth and space,
As though the spring itself withheld from me.

Come forth! The hawthorn blooms in white array,
The meadows blaze with buttercups and light;
April's pale charms have had their fading day—
'Tis May now bids thee welcome her delight.

And more than season's turn compels my call:
This month thou steppest into womanhood's door,
One-and-twenty years, a milestone tall,
A day of honor come but once, no more.

Shall such a birthday pass without thy friend
Beside thee, sharing in the joy it brings?
Nay, let no wall, no duty, no pretend
Delay the flight on which glad friendship wings.

For every hour that early summer lends
Is treasure spent before the bloom is gone;
The rose that opens rarely twice attends—
Come, Jane, before the fleeting splendor's drawn

Into the past, where wishes idly lie,
And we lament the day we let it pass.
Leave now Augusta's walls, beneath this sky,
And meet me where the May shines bright at last.
outputs.L5:
# Now, And, Why

**Now** is the only moment we ever truly inhabit. The past has already slipped beyond our grasp, existing only as memory and reconstruction. The future remains a realm of possibility, forever just out of reach. Yet the present—this fleeting, ever-renewing instant—is where all of life actually happens. We breathe now. We think now. We choose now. Every plan we make for tomorrow, every regret we carry from yesterday, is processed through the lens of this singular, precious moment.

**And** is the word of connection, of continuation, of accumulation. It links one thought to another, one experience to the next. Life rarely consists of isolated events; instead, it unfolds as a chain of "ands"—we wake up *and* we work, we love *and* we lose, we learn *and* we grow. This small conjunction carries the weight of narrative itself. Without "and," stories would fragment into disconnected fragments, unable to build toward meaning. It is the thread that stitches together the fabric of our days into something resembling a coherent life.

**Why** is perhaps the most human of all questions. It is the engine of curiosity, the root of philosophy, the spark behind every scientific discovery and every act of self-reflection. Children ask "why" incessantly, testing the boundaries of understanding. Adults often stop asking as frequently, yet the question never truly disappears—it simply goes underground, surfacing in moments of crisis or wonder. Why do we suffer? Why do we love? Why does anything exist at all? These questions may never receive final answers, but the act of asking them is itself transformative. It pushes us beyond mere existence into the realm of meaning-making.

Together, these three words form a kind of quiet meditation on being alive: we exist in the **now**, connected through the **and** of experience, driven forward by the eternal **why**. Perhaps wisdom lies not in resolving these tensions, but in learning to hold them simultaneously—present, connected, and endlessly curious.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Romantic-era style poem inviting a friend named Jane to leave the city and celebrate her 21st birthday in the countryside during spring.
counterfactuals.output:
# An Invitation to Jane, on Her One-and-Twentieth Spring

Come, Jane, and quit the city's smoke and stone,
Where Spring herself is but a rumor grown
Among the chimney-pots and crowded ways—
Come breathe with me these bright, untainted days.

The country calls thee with a thousand tongues:
The thrush that in the hawthorn-bush hath sung
Since dawn first broke in gold across the lea,
The brook that laughs its way toward the sea.

Thou hast but one-and-twenty years today—
A number sweet as blossoms in the May,
And should be met not in some crowded room,
But where the earth herself is quick with bloom.

Come let us climb the gentle rising hill
Where daffodils have drunk their fill
Of April rain, and now in golden crowds
Do nod their heads to slow, admiring clouds.

We'll find the meadow where the lambs at play
Do celebrate, unknowing, this thy day,
And thou shalt wear a wreath of woodbine white
Whilst I recite thy virtues with delight.

No candles need we, when the sun burns bright
And gilds the world entire in living light;
No walls to hold the warmth of friendship in—
The wide sky is our roof, the fields our inn.

So leave thy books, thy desk, thy narrow street,
And let the dewy grass receive thy feet.
Come celebrate the years that thou hast seen
Where all the world itself turns young and green.

For one-and-twenty summers thou hast known,
Yet spring, dear Jane, is ever but its own—
Eternal youth that needs no candle's flame:
Come, let us greet the season and thy name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a formal, old-fashioned English verse in the manner of Byron or Wordsworth, addressed to "Jane," urging her to leave "Augusta's walls" and enjoy May's arrival.
counterfactuals.output:
**To Jane, Upon the Coming of May**

Oh Jane! forsake Augusta's walls of stone,
Where mirth is measured out by candle-light,
And come where Nature holds her ancient throne,
Uncrowned by aught but morning's tender light.

The winter's chains are broken from the streams,
That leap in silver o'er the waking lea;
And soft the willow bends, as if in dreams
Of some far Eden it would have thee see.

What are the gilded rooms, the whispered praise,
The candled mirrors and the measured dance,
To one pale primrose, opening its face
Beneath the sun's most unrehearsed glance?

Come forth, sweet maid, while yet the hawthorn blows,
And May her fragrant coronal doth twine;
Leave thou the world its pomp, its studied shows—
The lark's plain music shall be more divine.

I know a bank where cowslips take their rest,
And violets steal the color from thine eyes;
There let us wander, if thou deem'st it best,
Beneath the arch of yon unclouded skies.

For what is life, if pent in chambers dim,
While all without doth burgeon and rejoice?
Thou wert not made for walls so cold and grim,
But for the meadow's breath and April's voice.

Then quit, O Jane, those grey and guarded towers,
Where custom chains the spirit as it will;
Come taste with me the freedom of the hours,
And let thy heart, too long subdued, be still—

Still but with peace, not sorrow; for the May
Hath in her keeping such a balm for pain
As cities know not, howsoever gay—
Come, let us seek the living world again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a poem imitating early 1800s poetic diction, with references to zephyrs, violets, and May, persuading a young woman to visit the writer before her birthday passes?
counterfactuals.output:
**To Celia, Ere Her Natal Day Be Flown**

O come, sweet maid, while yet the hours
Are soft with May's benignant breath,
While zephyrs stir the waking flowers
And meadows wear no sign of death.

The violets, in their purple best,
Have donned their crowns beside the stream,
And linger, as if loath to rest
Beneath a sun's more ardent beam.

Come now, before the fleeting days
Have borne thy natal morn away—
Before the sun's more searching rays
Do steal the gentle bloom of May.

I know not what the summer brings,
Nor what the autumn winds may say,
But this I know: on zephyr's wings
Time carries youth's sweet hours away.

Then let not distance, nor delay,
Nor cold reserve, thy coming stay—
Come, ere thy blessed natal day
Hath faded like the flowers of May.

For what are violets, what is spring,
If thou wilt not their beauty share?
Come, let thy laughter round me ring,
And make even Maytime doubly fair.

So haste, dear Celia, swift as thought,
Ere time hath stol'n thy day of birth—
The fairest gift that May hath brought
Is thy dear presence here on earth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a rhyming, iambic poem about longing for a friend's visit as spring turns to May, culminating in a birthday invitation to turn twenty-one.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Season's Ask**

The frost has fled, the buds appear,
the world wakes soft in green and gold,
but still no word from you, my dear—
the days grow warm, the wait grows old.

I watch the crocus break the ground
and robins test their throats again,
yet still I miss that welcome sound
of footsteps on the path, old friend.

The daffodils have had their turn,
the tulips bow and start to fade,
and still this quiet ache will burn
for company that spring has stayed.

Now May arrives with fuller light,
the calendar turns page by page—
I count the days until the night
I mark another year of age.

So come, and let this ask be plain:
I'll turn twenty-one this month of May.
Don't let the miles or spring's slow rain
keep you from sharing in that day.

I'll save a seat, I'll light the cake,
I'll hold the door until you're near—
for twenty-one's too much to make
without my oldest, dearest, here.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical, antiquated English poem lamenting April's passing and celebrating May's arrival, ending with a personal plea for someone named Jane to come celebrate her coming-of-age birthday.
counterfactuals.output:
**Upon the Turning of April to May, and a Plea to Jane**

Farewell, sweet April, thou fickle maid,
Whose tears and smiles were interlaid;
Thy showers soft did wake the earth,
And coax the timid snowdrop's birth.
Now thou dost fade like morning mist,
By fairer Maytime's warmth dismissed—
Yet shall thy memory linger long,
Enshrined within the thrushes' song.

Farewell, thou month of fickle skies,
Where sun and rain in swift surprise
Did chase each other o'er the lea,
And left their tears on every tree.
Thou wert the herald, not the king,
The tender prelude unto spring;
Thy work is done, thy hour is spent,
Go thou in peace, thou softly went.

Now hail, O May, in verdant dress,
Thou come to crown the earth's largesse!
The hawthorn breaks in bridal white,
The meadows swim in golden light.
The cuckoo calls from hidden bower,
The bee doth seek the opening flower,
And all the world, in green arrayed,
Doth celebrate thy bright parade.

Thou bringest warmth where cold did reign,
Thou driest up the lingering rain,
And on thy brow a crown thou wears
Of blossoms pale and sun-kissed airs.
The very brooks do seem to sing
In gladness for thy blossoming,
And every heart that beats below
Doth quicken at thy tender glow.

But O, sweet May, thou bringest more
Than bud and bloom to field and shore—
For in thy course a day doth stand
Most dear, most marked by Fate's own hand:
The day when Jane, in youth's fair flower,
Shall greet her twenty-first bright hour,
And step across that golden line
Where girlhood's dreams to womanhood combine.

Come, Jane, as May herself doth come,
With laughter bright and gladness, some
To share the joy this season brings,
While all around, the springtime sings.
Leave off thy tasks, thy cares lay by,
Beneath this warm and welcoming sky,
And let us raise our voices high
To toast the year that draweth nigh.

Come, dearest Jane, no more delay,
Come celebrate thy flowering day;
As April yields to May's embrace,
So childhood yields to woman's grace.
Come, let thy laughter fill the air,
Come, let us crown thee flower-fair,
For thou and May, in sweet array,
Together bloom this blessed day.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
